title: Growth on growth
objectives: Apply a percentage change repeatedly with a power of the multiplier
Turn a run of returns into a cumulative return

screens.title: Growth on growth
screens.prose: Money left to grow earns growth on its earlier growth. We will see how fast that adds up, and how it differs from adding the same amount each year.
You save £1,000.00 at 10% interest a year. Interest is added at the end of each year and left in the account. After one year you have £1,100.00.
screens.question: Set the Year 2 bar to the balance after two years.

hints.text: Year 2's interest is 10% of the balance at the start of year 2.
Year 2 starts from £1,100.00.
10% of £1,100.00 is £110.00, so the balance becomes £1,210.00.

feedback.correct: Year 2 earns £110.00, not £100.00, because it starts from £1,100.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take 10% of the Year 1 balance and add it on.

byKey.simple: You added £100.00 again. Year 2's 10% is taken from £1,100.00, so it earns £110.00.

explain.text: Year 2's interest is 10% of £1,100.00, which is £110.00. The extra £10.00 is interest on the first year's interest. In one move: $1000 \times 1.1 \times 1.1 = 1210$.

screens.prose: Keep going. Each year's interest is 10% of that year's starting balance.

state.caption: Years 3 and 4 are yours to fill in

screens.question: Fill in years 3 and 4.

hints.text: Each year starts with the balance the year before ended on.
Year 3 starts at £1,210.00.
Year 3: interest £121.00, end £1,331.00. Year 4 starts at £1,331.00 and earns £133.10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take 10% of each year's start, add it on, and carry the end into the next year.

byKey.r2c2: Year 3's interest is 10% of £1,210.00, the balance it starts with.
byKey.r3c1: Year 4 starts with the balance year 3 ended on.

explain.text: Each year's interest is 10% of a bigger balance, so the interest itself grows. That is **compound** growth: growth on growth. Every year multiplies the balance by 1.1.

canvas.caption: Each bar is 1.1 times the one before

screens.prose: Each year multiplies the balance by 1.1, so after $n$ years it is $1000 \times 1.1^n$. Adding £100.00 a year instead is called **simple** interest.
screens.question: What is the compound balance after 5 years?

hints.text: How many times is the balance multiplied by 1.1?
Year 5 is one more 10% on £1,464.10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by 1.1 once for each year.

byKey.simple: You added £100.00 a year: that is simple interest. Each year's 10% is of a growing balance, so it earns more.
byKey.times-n: You multiplied by 1.1 times 5. Five years apply 1.1 five times over: $1.1^5$.

explain.text: Five years multiply by 1.1 five times: $1000 \times 1.1^5 = 1610.51$. Simple interest gives £1,500.00. The extra £110.51 is interest earned on interest.

screens.prose: A new account. £2,500.00 earns 4% a year, compounded, for 2 years.
screens.question: What is the balance after 2 years?

hints.text: Each year multiplies by 1.04.
Year 2's interest is 4% of £2,600.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by 1.04 for each year.

byKey.simple: You added £100.00 twice. Year 2's 4% is of £2,600.00, which is £104.00.
byKey.one-year: That is the balance after one year. Apply 1.04 once more.

explain.text: $1.04^2 = 1.0816$, so the balance is £2,704.00. Simple interest would give £2,700.00. Over two years the gap is only £4.00: compounding starts slowly.

screens.prose: Compounding works on falls too. A share at £50.00 falls 10% a day for three days.
screens.question: Set the Day 3 bar to the close after the third fall.

hints.text: Day 3's fall is 10% of Day 2's close.
Day 3 starts from £40.50.
10% of £40.50 is £4.05, so Day 3 closes at £36.45.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take 10% of Day 2's close off Day 2's close.

byKey.simple: You took 30% off £50.00. Each day's 10% is of a smaller price, so the falls shrink: £5.00, £4.50, £4.05.
byKey.pounds: You took £5.00 off again. The third fall is 10% of £40.50, which is £4.05.

explain.text: $50 \times 0.9^3 = 36.45$: a fall of 27.1%, not 30%. Each fall is 10% of a smaller price, so the falls shrink. Repeated 10% falls never reach £0.00.

screens.prose: A fund advert says: 10% a year for 10 years doubles your money, because ten lots of 10% make 100%. The line shows the advert's sum.
screens.question: With 10% a year compounded, what does £1,000.00 grow to in 10 years?

options.why: You added ten lots of 10% of £1,000.00, as the advert did. Each year's 10% is of a bigger balance.
You multiplied 1.1 by 10. Ten years apply 1.1 ten times over: $1.1^{10}$.

hints.text: How many times is the balance multiplied by 1.1?
The straight line adds £100.00 a year: that is the advert's sum.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply 1.1 once for each of the ten years.

byKey.advert: You added the ten 10% rises, as the advert did. Compounding multiplies by 1.1 ten times, which is about 2.59, not 2.

explain.text: Ten years multiply by $1.1^{10} \approx 2.594$, so £1,000.00 grows to £2,593.74. Adding percentages gives simple interest, £2,000.00. Over long periods, adding percentages badly understates compound growth.

screens.prose: A balance $P$ grows by a fraction $r$ each period for $n$ periods. $$\text{compound: } P(1 + r)^n \qquad \text{simple: } P(1 + nr)$$ Compound multiplies by $(1 + r)$ each period. Simple adds $Pr$ each period.
screens.question: £500.00 earns 6% a year, compounded, for 3 years. Which calculation gives the balance?

options.why: You added 6% three times. That is simple interest.
You multiplied by 3 instead of applying 1.06 three times.
You compounded the rate alone. Each year multiplies by $1 + r = 1.06$.

hints.text: Which factor is applied once per year?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by $(1 + r)$ once for each year.

explain.text: $500 \times 1.06^3 = 595.508$, about £595.51. Simple interest would give $500 \times 1.18 = 590$, which is £590.00.

screens.prose: Where does the power come from? Build the compound formula one year at a time.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: After 1 year: $P(1 + r)$, one change is one multiplication
After 2 years: $P(1 + r) \times (1 + r) = P(1 + r)^2$, year 2 multiplies year 1's balance
After 3 years: $P(1 + r)^2 \times (1 + r) = P(1 + r)^3$, the same step again
After $n$ years: $P(1 + r)^n$, one factor of $(1 + r)$ for each year

hints.text: Which line needs no earlier year?
Each year multiplies the balance the year before ended with.
Year 1, then year 2 from year 1, then year 3 from year 2, then the pattern.

feedback.correct: Each year adds one more factor of $(1 + r)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line builds on the year before.

byKey.f3: Year 3 builds on year 2's balance, so it comes after year 2.
byKey.f4: The pattern for $n$ years comes from the cases before it, so it goes last.

explain.text: Each year multiplies the previous balance by $(1 + r)$, so the factors pile up into a power. Simple interest adds $Pr$ each year instead, giving $P(1 + nr)$. The extra in the power is interest on interest.

screens.prose: A trading signal holds a stock for three weeks. Its weekly returns are +5%, −4% and +2.5%. A report adds them and claims +3.5%.
screens.question: What is the true return over the three weeks? Give a percentage.

hints.text: Turn each weekly return into a multiplier.
The three multipliers are 1.05, 0.96 and 1.025.
$1.05 \times 0.96 \times 1.025 = 1.0332$. Take away 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the three multipliers, then take away 1.

byKey.added: You added the weekly returns, as the report did. Returns compound: multiply the multipliers, then take away 1.
byKey.multiplier: 103.32% is the final value as a share of the start. The return is that minus 100%.

explain.text: $1.05 \times 0.96 \times 1.025 = 1.0332$, a **cumulative return** of 3.32%. The stock went from £200.00 to £206.64, which agrees. Adding returns ignores growth on growth, so here it overstates.

ideas: Repeated percentage changes multiply: $n$ periods of growth $r$ multiply by $(1 + r)^n$.
Simple interest adds the same amount each period; compound interest earns interest on interest.
Returns compound. Multiply the multipliers and take away 1; adding the returns is only an approximation.
summary.trap: Adding percentages over time. Ten years at 10% is ×2.59, not ×2.

quiz.prose: £800.00 earns 5% a year, compounded, for 2 years.
quiz.question: What is the balance?

options.why: You added 5% of £800.00 twice. Year 2's 5% is of £840.00.
That is the balance after one year. Apply 1.05 once more.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by 1.05 for each year.

quiz.prose: A price falls 20% a year for 2 years.
quiz.question: What is the overall percentage fall?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the two multipliers, then compare with 1.

byKey.added: You added the two 20% falls. The second is 20% of a smaller price.
byKey.kept: 64% is what is left. The fall is the 36% that went.

explain.text: $0.8 \times 0.8 = 0.64$, so the price keeps 64% and falls 36%. Repeated falls shrink because each is taken from a smaller price.

quiz.prose: A £10,000.00 fund grows 6% in a year. Then a 1% fee is taken from the balance.
quiz.question: What is the balance after the fee?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the growth, then the fee on the grown balance.

byKey.subtract: You took 1% from 6% and grew the fund by 5%. The fee is 1% of £10,600.00, which is £106.00.

explain.text: The fund grows to £10,600.00, and the fee is 1% of that, £106.00. So the balance is $10000 \times 1.06 \times 0.99 = 10494$. Fees compound too: they come off the grown balance.

quiz.prose: Two accounts run for 3 years. One pays 10% a year compounded. The other pays 11% a year simple.
quiz.question: Which ends with more?

options.why: You compared the rates only. Compound gives $1.1^3 = 1.331$; simple gives $1 + 3 \times 0.11 = 1.33$.
Close, but 1.331 is above 1.33. On £1,000.00 that is £1.00 more.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out both multipliers.

explain.text: Compound: $1.1^3 = 1.331$. Simple: $1 + 3 \times 0.11 = 1.33$. Over longer periods compounding pulls further ahead.
